passages.original: quoties festi dies occurrebant, id est Sabbato ac die Dominico, in unum congregati, hymnos apte ad suam haeresim compositos, alternatim sibi respondentes canebant, nocturnis scilicet ac matutinis horis. » llunc vero alternum cantum Socrates antiphonarium, ἀντίϕωνον ύμνωδίαν appellat; unde antiphonæ, quae ad alternum psalmorum cantum præcinuntur, nomen retinuerunt.
passages.english: whenever feast days came round, that is, on the Sabbath and on the Lord's Day, they gathered together and sang hymns composed to suit their heresy, answering one another in alternation, namely at the night and morning hours." This alternating chant Socrates calls "antiphonal," *antiphōnos hymnōdia* [antiphonal hymn-singing]; from this the antiphons, which are intoned before the alternating chanting of the psalms, have kept their name.
passages.notes: "llunc" is a scanning error for "Hunc". The sentence begins mid-clause, continuing a quotation from Socrates (Ecclesiastical History VI.8) about the Arians, "who each week...". The phrase "antiphonarium" is rendered "antiphonal".

passages.original: omnes loquuntur, et nullus obstrepit. » Itaque cum lector Scripturas recitaret, vix impelrari poterat silentium ; cum vero psalmus cantaretur, obst repebat nemo, quoniam omnes cantu occupati eraM. Hujusce ritus originem describit sanctus Augustinus in lib. IX Confessionum, cap. 7 : « Non longe cœperat Mediolanensis Ecclesia genus hoc consolationiset exhortationis celebrAre, magno studio fratrum concinentium vocibus et cordibus, Nimiram annus eft, aut non multo amplius, cum just na,Valentiniani regis pueri mater, hominem tuum Ambrosium perseque- retur hæresis suæ causa, qua fuerat seducta ab Arianis. Excubabat pia plebs in ecclesia,mori parata cum episcopo servo tuo...
passages.english: all speak, and no one makes a disturbance." So when the reader was reciting the Scriptures, silence could scarcely be obtained; but when a psalm was sung, no one made a disturbance, since all were occupied with the singing. Saint Augustine describes the origin of this rite in Book IX of the Confessions, chapter 7: "Not long before, the Church of Milan had begun to practise this kind of consolation and exhortation, with the brethren singing together with great zeal of voice and heart. It was indeed a year, or not much more, since Justina, mother of the boy-king Valentinian, was persecuting your servant Ambrose on account of her heresy, into which she had been led astray by the Arians. The devout people kept watch in the church, ready to die with their bishop, your servant...
passages.notes: Several scanning errors silently corrected (impetrari, obstrepebat, erant, consolationis et, celebrare, Nimirum, est, Justina).

passages.original: 14. Quæ superius ex cantu psalmorum Mediolani instituto sibi accidisse narrat Augustinus, ab baptismi ipsius tempus, id est ad annum 387 referenda sunt. Eumdem ritum in Africam ipse invexit episcopus. Alternum porro fuisse colligimus es ejus enarratione in psalmum XXVI, num. 1 : « Voces istae psalmi, quas audivimus, et ex parte canlavimus, » etc.
passages.english: 14. What Augustine relates above as having happened to him from the singing of psalms instituted at Milan is to be referred to the time of his baptism, that is, to the year 387. He himself, as bishop, brought the same rite into Africa. We gather, moreover, that it was alternating from his exposition of Psalm 26, no. 1: "These words of the psalm, which we have heard and in part sung," etc.
passages.notes: 'ab baptismi' read as 'ad baptismi'; 'es' as 'ex'; 'canlavimus' as 'cantavimus'.

passages.original: » Alius igitur erat tunc in Ecclesia ritus, q"ando Alexandrinum Augustitnus præfe rcbat. Denique in Africa psalmis etiam intermiscebantur certis diebus lectiones, « quæ ita eraut annuæ, et aliae esse non possent, » ait idem Augustinus initio expositionis in primam Joannis. In concilio Carthaginensi in statuitur canone 47 : Ut præter Scripturas canonica, nihil in ecclesia legatur sub nomine dicina- tum Scripturarum. Quæ clausula non excludit tractatus sanctorum Patrum, nec lectiones martyrum passionum, quas legi permittit concilium Africanum, cum anniversarii diu corum celebrantur.
passages.english: " So there was then a different rite in the Church, when Augustine preferred the Alexandrian one. Finally, in Africa readings were also interspersed with the psalms on certain days, readings "which were so fixed for the year that there could not be others," as the same Augustine says at the beginning of his exposition of the First [Epistle] of John. In the Council of Carthage it is laid down in canon 47: That apart from the canonical Scriptures nothing be read in church under the name of the divine Scriptures. This clause does not exclude the treatises of the holy Fathers, nor the readings of the passions of the martyrs, which the African council permits to be read when their anniversary days are celebrated.
passages.notes: 'dicinarum' read as 'divinarum'; 'diu corum' as 'dies eorum'; stray 'in' before 'statuitur' omitted.

passages.original: Psalmorum hic modulator et phonascus, Ante altaria, fratre gratulante, instructas docuit sonare classes. Hic solemoibus annuis paravit, Quæ quo tempore'tecta convenirent. Secundum Claudianum, divini in illa Ecclesia officii amplificator censendus est sanctus Cæsarius episcopus, teste Cypriano episcopo Tolonensi in libro primo de ejus Vita. Sic enim legitur num. 10 ;« De profectibus itaque cunctorum sollicitus et providus Pastor statim instituit ut quotidie Tertiae, Sextæque, et Nonæ opus in sancti Stephani basilica clerici cum hymnis cantarent ;
passages.english: This modulator and voice-trainer of the psalms, before the altars, with his brother rejoicing, taught the drilled choirs to sing. He arranged for the yearly solemnities what should be fitting at each season. After Claudianus, Saint Caesarius the bishop is to be reckoned the enlarger of the divine office in that Church, as Bishop Cyprian of Toulon testifies in the first book of his Life. For thus we read in no. 10: "Therefore the shepherd, solicitous and provident for the progress of all, at once established that every day the clergy should sing the office of Terce, Sext and None in the basilica of Saint Stephen with hymns;
passages.notes: The opening is verse (Sidonius' epitaph of Claudianus). 'Quae quo tempore tecta convenirent' is corrupt as printed; the sense 'what suited each season' is conjectural (Sidonius reads 'quae quo tempore lecta convenirent', 'which readings suited which season').

passages.original: hac vero glurificatione Trinitatis tantummodo solere antiphonas terminari, » id est, si bene interpretor, cantum alternum. Nam buuc antiphonae nomine apud antiquiores auctores intelligi 406 superius vidimus. Alter locus est in lib. in, cap. 4, ubi duo nos docet Cassianus. Primum, matutinam solemnitatem, id est Laudes, < expletis nocturnis psalmis et orationibus, post modicum temporis intervallum, > in Galliæ monasteriis fuisse celebratam. Quod etiam in regula sua præcipit sanctus Benedictus ; atque de Emeritensi Ecclesia hiemis tempore in more fuisse tradit Paulus Diaconus in lib. de Patribus Emeritensibus, cap. i. Secundum est, alteram < matutinam solemnitatem , > quod Primæ officium est, < in occiduis vel maxime regionibus » observatam. I Et tamen Cæsarius, ut modo vidimus , Cassiano inferior aetate, nullam Primæ facit mentionem ;
passages.english: but that antiphons are customarily ended only with this glorification of the Trinity," that is, if I interpret rightly, alternating chant. For we saw above that this is meant by the name antiphon among the older authors. The other passage is in Book III, chapter 4, where Cassian teaches us two things. First, that the morning solemnity, that is Lauds, was celebrated in the monasteries of Gaul "after the night psalms and prayers were finished, following a short interval of time." This Saint Benedict also prescribes in his Rule; and Paul the Deacon reports in his book on the Fathers of Mérida, chapter 1, that it was the custom in the Church of Mérida in wintertime. The second is that another "morning solemnity," which is the office of Prime, was observed "especially in the western regions." And yet Caesarius, as we have just seen, later in date than Cassian, makes no mention of Prime;

passages.original: Hæc fere sunt quae de Lugdunensi, Viennensi, Arelatensi, aliisque vicinis ecclesiis nobis observanda occurrerunt : ex quibus intelligimus, primo quidem psalmos ab uno lectore aliquando fuisse recitatos, testante Cassiano, et post finem singulorum versiculorum Gloria Patri ab omnibus cantatum; deinde vero eam psalmodiae disciplinam successisse, ut omnes canerent, quod Caesarius Arelate vicinarum Ecclesiarum exemplo instituit.
passages.english: These are roughly the things that came to our notice concerning the churches of Lyon, Vienne, Arles and other neighbouring churches. From them we understand, first, that the psalms were at one time recited by a single reader, as Cassian testifies, and that after the end of each verse the Gloria Patri was sung by all; and then that there followed that discipline of psalmody whereby all sang, which Caesarius instituted at Arles following the example of neighbouring Churches.

passages.original: Huic inter primos psalmodie originem esse tribuendam conjiciebam, tum ex eo quod in Phrygiam ob catholicam fidem relegatus, hunc psallendi morem ex Asia in Galliam facile invehere potuit : tum quia Latinorum primus librum hymnorum composoit, teste Hieronymo, et post cum Isidoro. Exciderunt hymni illi; sed eos viderat Dieronymus, ex quo discimus, in hymnorum carmine Gallos indociles ab Hilario vocari, ut ipse Hieronymus testatur in praefatione libri II commentarii ad Galatas. Unus ex his integer bymnus inter Hilarii opera nobis reliquus est, iambicis versibus constans, qui filiae ejus Abræ missus dicitur. In eo hymno fit mentio Matutinae, cui horae is aptatus est.
passages.english: I conjectured that the origin of psalmody should be attributed to him among the first, both because, having been banished to Phrygia for the Catholic faith, he could easily bring this manner of psalm-singing from Asia into Gaul, and because he was the first of the Latins to compose a book of hymns, as Jerome testifies, and after him Isidore. Those hymns are lost; but Jerome had seen them, from whom we learn that the Gauls were called unteachable in hymn-singing by Hilary, as Jerome himself testifies in the preface to Book II of the commentary on Galatians. One complete hymn of these remains to us among Hilary's works, consisting of iambic verses, which is said to have been sent to his daughter Abra. In that hymn mention is made of Matins, to which hour it was fitted.

passages.original: Sed quoniam humana imbecillitas, atque adeo multiplex hujusce vitae necessitas non patitur ut homines continua mentis intentione in Dei ,laudibus et oratione occupentur; imo etiam Deo magis acceptum sit ut clerici aliis ordinis sui officiis, quae proximi caritas exigit, identidem incumbant ; ideo « diversas orandi horas, » ut Hieronymus ad Eustochium loquitur, « habere debent, ut si forte aliquo fuerint opere nimium detenti, ipsum eos ad officium tempus admoneat. Atque hoc demum pacto jugis orationis praeceptum implere possunt, ex Augustino, « si nullo die intermittantur opera orandi. » Porro, ut idem sanctus Doctor ait in epistola ad Probam, « ideo per certa intervalla horarum ac temporum etiam verbis rogamus Deum, ut ipsis rerum signis nos acrius excitemus.
passages.english: But since human weakness, and indeed the manifold necessity of this life, does not allow men to be occupied in the praises of God and prayer with continuous attention of mind, and indeed it is even more acceptable to God that clerics should from time to time apply themselves to the other duties of their order which love of neighbour demands, therefore they "ought to have different hours for praying," as Jerome says to Eustochium, "so that if they are perhaps too detained by some work, the time itself may remind them of their duty." And in this way at last they can fulfil the precept of continual prayer, according to Augustine, "if no day the works of praying are interrupted." Moreover, as the same holy Doctor says in the letter to Proba, "we therefore at fixed intervals of hours and seasons also ask God in words, so that by these very signs of things we may rouse ourselves more keenly.

passages.original: Nam ut omittam id quod de Equitio abbate narrat Gregorius Magnus, qui Equitius « sacros Codices in pelliciis sacculis dextro laevoque latere portare solebat, > quod etiam de Fructuoso episcopo Braoarensi legimus, 434 Gregorius IX de monacbis foras profecturis id statuit, < ut ipsi horas dicant in via, et de libris provideatur iisdem. » Id generis duos pro itinerantibus Codices in sacrario Cisterciensi aliquando vidimus, quos hoc modo describit Josephus Meglingerus in Itinere suo Cisterciensi : < Libelli trium digitorum latitudinem non excedunt, plus tamen longitudinis habent. Dum clausos aspicis, parvi apparent; at aperti triplo majores evadunt, foliis, quae ex membrana rudi constant, ter complicatis, deorsum, et ambobus lateribus.
passages.english: For, to pass over what Gregory the Great relates of the abbot Equitius, that Equitius "used to carry the sacred books in leather bags on his right and left side," which we also read of Fructuosus, bishop of Braga, Gregory IX laid down concerning monks about to travel abroad "that they should say the hours on the road, and be provided with books." We once saw two books of this kind for travellers in the sacristy of Cîteaux, which Joseph Meglinger describes thus in his Cistercian Journey: "The little books do not exceed three fingers in width, but have more length. When you look at them closed they seem small; but opened they become three times larger, the leaves, made of rough parchment, being folded three times, downward and on both sides.
